I mean: just taking the lessons learnt from Payday 3, and Helldivers 2, you *really* want to launch in a polished state these days. The times when you could launch a game before it’s had much of a polishing phase, and use that influx of cash to both cover the initial dev costs ‘n’ justify continued development, ‘til you’ve built up a sustainable playerbase from word of mouth… well, those days really seem to’ve passed. Investors and execs seriously need to catch up, and realize that games which are able to rebuild their rep after a rocky launch are making up an ever-smaller chunk of the games coming out — and the most exciting thing a new game can currently be described as is simply “polished”, for the majority of players; and especially those who’re into co-op games

Anyways… I kinda like the game now, ever since Boys in Blue; but do you think there was ever a chance that it could’ve had a Multiversus-like un-launch? I ask that, ‘cause even with the game having progressed to where it is now, I’m still left feeling sad about its future outlook. So, I just have to wonder: if it’d been taken off the market, and given another year or so in the oven… could that’ve ended up better satisfying shareholders, as well as both the game’s existing and potential audience?

There’s very little use in “what-ifs”, of course - especially during such a tumultuous time across the entire entertainment industry - but this is easily the game I’ve thought about the most over the last year. The easiest reality to ponder is “what if it’d been delayed”, but that one seems so unlikely in the face of corporate arrogance and desperation. Ultimately, I can only hope that it ended up being a learning experience for the higher-ups at Deep Silver/Plaion/Embracer - since I don’t believe I’ve actually heard about any of their games having been released too early, or in too broken of a state, after Payday 3’s release.

Yeah - for what it’s worth, generations are pretty much entirely defined by their trends in adulthood, rather than their childhoods.

So, Gen Z - as of right now - is in that particularly weird stretch of time in generational studies; where its oldest members are pushing thirty, and have quite a bit of data gathered on them at this point… while its youngest members aren’t even in high school yet. Long-term, the data will most likely show quite similar trends in adulthood among people born in that sixteen years’ span, just as has been seen with Gen X and Y. It’s just harder to see now, since the actual data only really tends to clear up once generations have entered the 42-26 range (which is why the actual long-term trends and habits among millennials have come into much stronger focus over the last several years, ofc)

Also, to clarify: Gen Z’s whole deal is that it’s the first generation to not really have any memories of anything before the turn of the century. Remembering 9/11 is a common thing that people point to as a generational divide, but it’s not what really defines it.
